extracted.intended_audience: computer scientists and mathematicians (CS 209 students) learning technical/mathematical writing and copy-editing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing clear, well-organized mathematical and technical exposition (lectures/handouts/papers), including diction, syntax, symbols, and organization. Extracted from CS 209 class notes and guest lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability grade (linear formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The style routine produces a 'grade' computed as grade = α (words/sentence) + β (syllables/word) + γ, where α, β, γ are determined by linear regression against sample texts with assigned subjective grade levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the computed grade as an indicator of education level needed to read the piece; be aware it's based only on words/sentence and syllables/word and may miss musical or stylistic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to minimise grade level (with restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don's usual aim is to minimise the grade level indicated by readability indices, although overdoing simplification can defeat the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek low grade-level readability for clarity, but avoid oversimplifying technical content or sacrificing necessary precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style-analysis diagnostics
rubrics_metrics.description: The program outputs average sentence length, percentage of very short/long sentences, sentence classifications, and percentages of nouns/adjectives/verbs (active or passive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these statistics to spot imbalances (too many long sentences, excessive passive voice, paucity of adjectives) and to inform targeted revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive-voice detection
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence is considered 'passive' if a passive verb appears anywhere in it, even in a subclause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware this flag can be coarse; examine flagged sentences to decide if passive voice is acceptable or should be rewritten in active voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expletive classification ('It...' or 'There...')
rubrics_metrics.description: Style classifies any sentence beginning with 'It...' or 'There...' as an 'expletive' sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such sentences cautiously — they may be stylistically weak or may be legitimate depending on context (e.g., historical usage, idiom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction filter (flag questionable words/phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: A diction program has a dictionary of ~450 'questionable' words/phrases (e.g., 'gratuitous', 'number of', 'due to', 'very', 'literally') and flags them for reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider suggested alternatives but apply judgment — users accept about 50% of diction's suggestions; some flagged items (e.g., 'due to' in mathematics) may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect field-specific usages (e.g., 'due to')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some flagged words/phrases (like 'due to') have legitimate specialized uses in mathematics/science ('This theorem, due to Cauchy...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diction/suggested changes conflict with standard technical usage, retain the field-appropriate form and document consistency choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weak intensifiers ('very')
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice: avoid 'very' unless it truly strengthens the sentence — suggested test: would you use a stronger swear ('damn') in its place?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stronger, more specific words rather than generic intensifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague/colloquial modifiers ('really', 'pretty', 'actually', 'in fact')
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'really' or 'pretty' often add vagueness in technical writing and should be replaced with more precise phrasing or removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences to specify the substantive condition (example given: 'saving the computation for those vertices where the additional work contributes more to the visual quality').

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise and delete unnecessary phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut whole phrases or words that add no meaning (e.g., 'he has heard', 'the reason for removing the spaces from the list is that...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct constructions ('We remove the spaces because...') and eliminate verbosity that distracts readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer more questions than you raise
rubrics_metrics.description: A hallmark of good writing is that it answers more questions than it raises; sentences should not leave the reader wondering who/what/why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check sentences for implicit questions (e.g., 'cheaper than what?') and supply necessary clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep subject and verb proximate
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid separating subject and verb by many intervening words — such sentences are hard to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rearrange or shorten clauses so the subject and verb appear nearer each other for clearer comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer short sentences over long ones; use semicolons sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut long sentences where possible; a semicolon should be used only where separated clauses have a very close relationship, and often a period is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periods to improve pacing and clarity; avoid '19th-century mustiness' conveyed by overuse of semicolons (quote from Zinsser).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition and overused filler words
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated words like 'this', 'they', 'just', 'then' can be overused and cause monotony or confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read aloud to detect over-uses; vary wording or restructure sentences to avoid repetitive fillers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conversational idioms and awkward formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'Anyway,...', 'pretty straightforward', or clumsy constructs like 'again iterate through' are undesirable in formal technical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, formal phrasing appropriate to the intended venue (newspaper vs technical journal may differ in tone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer subject-verb-object style to reduce distractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many problems and over-use of passive voice are avoided if writers stick to a straightforward S-V-O style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active verbs and place the subject early to minimize reader distraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noise-phrases ('in the context of') are often removable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In the context of' is frequently a noise-phrase that can be deleted without loss of meaning, though sometimes it is necessary to signal topical continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate on a case-by-case basis: remove when redundant, keep when it helps the reader reorient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous pronoun references (e.g., 'It is unlikely...')
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that begin with 'It is unlikely...' or similar can leave the reader unsure of the referent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite to explicitly state the subject or restructure to avoid unclear pronoun references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch placement of 'only'
rubrics_metrics.description: Misplaced 'only' changes the meaning of sentences; placement must match intended emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check all possible placements when adding 'only' to ensure the sentence says what you mean (illustrated by many variants of 'I hit him in the eye yesterday').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid code-transliterated awkwardness (overuse of 'then')
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that result from translating code style ('if... then...') into prose can contain excessive 'then's and be awkward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite such sentences into clearer prose that does not mimic programming syntax unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept technical jargon where appropriate (e.g., 'object witnesses a property')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some constructions that sound odd in ordinary English may be standard and acceptable in computer science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give technical terms permission to evolve within the field; prioritize reader comprehension within the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with commonly confused word pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between 'prostrate'/'prostate', 'alternately'/'alternatively', 'imply'/'infer', 'disinterested'/'uninterested', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct word for the intended meaning to preserve semantic distinctions important to clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two basic rules: Do organize; Do not distract
rubrics_metrics.description: Paul Halmos' anchor rules: organize material and avoid distracting the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization and lack of distraction are overarching goals — use them as touchstones when editing and structuring exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four aspects of good mathematical communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider Semantics (words and meanings), Syntax (grammar), Symbols (notation), and Style (synthesis of the above).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance these aspects when writing math: precise word choice, grammatical clarity, careful symbol use, and coherent stylistic presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantics: resist careless change and imprecise usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid muddying meanings by misusing words (e.g., 'imply' vs 'infer', 'disinterested' vs 'uninterested', misuse of 'hopefully').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer preserving distinctions when writing for an audience that needs them; be aware that language changes but some confusions reduce clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax: grammar as organizational logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat grammar as providing logical structure (case, tense, person) that condenses information; ungrammatical forms distract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write grammatical sentences unless deliberately addressing an audience for whom nonstandard grammar is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and quotation marks: place logically
rubrics_metrics.description: Place quotation marks logically (Paul urges putting them where the logic of the sentence dictates rather than blindly following typographic convention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize logical placement of punctuation to reflect intended meaning; be mindful of stylistic/house conventions but aim for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending sentences with prepositions is not absolute taboo
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule against ending sentences with prepositions is 'reactionary grammarian balderdash' in many cases; some sentences are natural and clear with terminal prepositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not perform awkward gymnastics to avoid a terminal preposition; avoid only when it produces an awkward or ungrammatical sentence structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols: use numerals to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'one' could be a pronoun or a numeral, use '1' to indicate the numeral meaning and reduce ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explicit numeric notation where textual numerals might be ambiguous in mathematical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'we' and passive voice where possible; prefer imperative/indicative
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule #6 suggests using 'we' to avoid passive voice; Halmos prefers avoiding both 'we' and passive voice by using imperative or indicative moods and concise labels (e.g., 'Consequence: A implies B.', 'Replace x by 7 throughout.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'we' sparingly; choose direct commands or declarative short statements to reduce irrelevant tone and improve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not echo unusual words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repeating the same unusual word in unrelated passages because repetition can create unwarranted associations in readers' minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary vocabulary and avoid inadvertently linking distant parts of the exposition through repeated rare terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun/inclusivity choices should avoid distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over 'he' vs 'he or she' vs 'they': choices that draw attention away from content are undesirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a solution that maintains fluency and does not distract; consistency and minimal attention-drawing are priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proofs to proof by contradiction for exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction should not be used when a direct proof is available, because direct proofs are generally better expositionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While contradiction is useful for discovery, prefer direct arguments when writing for others; restructure stream-of-consciousness solution proofs for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization deserves the most writing time
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization is more than linear order; it involves weaving branches and alternative threads together. Paul spends most of his writing time on organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest significant effort in outlining and reorganizing material; study examples of organization at increasing complexity (thesaurus, encyclopedia, do-it-yourself article, textbook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules may be broken for rhetorical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: All rules are made to be broken: when you want to jar readers you may intentionally distract by changing notation or using ungrammatical sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break rules purposefully and sparingly, with awareness of the rhetorical effect and likely reader reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting and typography: prefer readable mathematical notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer clearer typographical representations (e.g., use slashed fraction form n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/3 instead of cramped stacked forms when readability suffers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When typesetting math, choose forms that maximize readability and prevent ambiguous parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-appropriate hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenation choices (e.g., 'programming-language notation' vs 'programming language notation') depend on disciplinary norms; in CS some hyphenation looks wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow conventions familiar to your audience; avoid over-hyphenation that disrupts customary phrasing in your field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split infinitives acceptable when they improve style
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to always avoid splitting infinitives is unwise; split infinitives can provide emphasis and forced rewrites may sound awkward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow split infinitives when they enhance clarity or tone; avoid dogmatic prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points should be used only with actual exclamations or interjections (e.g., 'Ouch!', 'Stop!'); some authorities don't note their use for surprise but creative solutions exist (parenthetical '!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exclamation points sparingly and purposefully; consider typographic tricks only when stylistically appropriate.
